claim: Ivermectin improves clinical outcomes in COVID-19

gate_trace.detail: excluded 1 study(ies) with documented integrity concerns
2 large RCT(s) show no effect; positive signal is smaller/older

ledger.citation: Reis 2022 New England Journal of Medicine
ledger.finding: TOGETHER platform RCT: early ivermectin in ~3,500 symptomatic high-risk outpatients did not reduce hospitalization/prolonged ED observation vs placebo; no benefit.
ledger.integrity_note: Large double-blind placebo-controlled adaptive platform trial; no integrity concerns.

ledger.finding: PRINCIPLE platform RCT (8,811 community adults): ivermectin gave no clinically meaningful faster recovery (HR ~1.15, below pre-specified 1.2 threshold) and no difference in hospitalization/death or 6-month recovery.
ledger.integrity_note: Large NIHR-funded open-label adaptive platform trial; no integrity concerns.

ledger.finding: I-TECH RCT (490 high-risk mild-to-moderate patients, Malaysia): ivermectin did not prevent progression to severe disease (21.6% vs 17.3%) and showed no secondary-outcome benefit.
ledger.integrity_note: Investigator-initiated multicenter RCT; no integrity concerns.

ledger.finding: Systematic review/meta-analysis of RCTs: ivermectin showed no significant effect on mortality, mechanical ventilation, or clinical improvement ('evidence beyond the hype' is null).
ledger.integrity_note: Post-hype synthesis; no integrity concerns.

ledger.finding: Early meta-analysis (RCTs, ~1,788 patients) reported ivermectin associated with reduced mortality; this pooled benefit was driven by trials later withdrawn/flagged (Elgazzar, Niaee) and does not survive clean re-analysis.
ledger.integrity_note: The meta-analysis itself is not retracted, but its positive signal depended on primary studies later withdrawn/questioned; illustrates fragility of the early pro-ivermectin evidence.

ledger.finding: Widely-cited preprint RCT claimed a large ivermectin mortality reduction and underpinned early positive meta-analyses. WITHDRAWN by Research Square (14 Jul 2021) for data-integrity/ethical concerns: duplicated patient records, deaths recorded before enrollment, and plagiarism.
ledger.integrity_note: Preprint withdrawn by Research Square for data-integrity/ethical concerns; never peer-reviewed yet drove early positive meta-analyses. Corroborated by Nature (d41586-021-02081-w) and multiple outlets.

ledger.citation: Shakhsi Niaee 2021 Asian Pacific Journal of Tropical Medicine
ledger.finding: Multicenter RCT (180 hospitalized adults) reported ivermectin sharply cut mortality vs controls; a positive study that fed pro-ivermectin meta-analyses. Data sleuths and an editorial note raised concerns over implausible baseline stratification/randomization; it is excluded from post-scrutiny meta-analyses.
ledger.integrity_note: Concerns raised informally (data sleuths, editorial note) over implausible baseline stratification; NOT a formal Expression of Concern — the journal stated the paper was not retracted and no retraction was pending. The formal EoCs were issued on downstream reviews (Kory; Bryant/Lawrie, Am J Ther), not on this primary study.

claim: Atorvastatin reduces LDL cholesterol in adults with hyperlipidemia

ledger.n: pooled double-blind RCTs of statins in hypercholesterolaemia (>=12 weeks)
ledger.finding: Dose-specific meta-analysis of double-blind RCTs: fixed-dose atorvastatin 10 mg lowered LDL-C by >30% from baseline (statins overall 24-49%), directly supporting atorvastatin's LDL-lowering effect in hypercholesterolaemia.
ledger.integrity_note: No retraction or expression of concern found.

ledger.n: 18 head-to-head trials (17 published + 1 unpublished; adults >=18 with elevated TC/LDL-C)
ledger.finding: Dose-specific meta-analysis of atorvastatin-vs-simvastatin head-to-head RCTs found atorvastatin produced significantly greater LDL-C reductions in the majority of dose comparisons (2-4x the potency of simvastatin) in hyperlipidemic adults.
ledger.integrity_note: No retraction or expression of concern found.

ledger.finding: Individual-patient-data pooled meta-analysis found atorvastatin 10-80 mg lowered LDL-C dose-dependently, with each doubling of dose giving ~4-6% further LDL-C reduction.
ledger.integrity_note: No retraction or expression of concern found.

ledger.finding: Prospective meta-analysis of 14 statin RCTs (including atorvastatin trials) achieved mean 1-year LDL-C differences up to 1.77 mmol/L, confirming statins robustly lower LDL-C; class-level anchor for atorvastatin's mechanism.
ledger.integrity_note: No retraction or expression of concern; only a standard 2005 erratum (Lancet 366(9494):1358).

ledger.n: 2,838 (type 2 diabetes, primary prevention, LDL-C <=4.14 mmol/L at entry)
ledger.finding: Placebo-controlled RCT of atorvastatin 10 mg/day lowered LDL-C and reduced major cardiovascular events by 37%; direct atorvastatin trial evidence, but the population is type 2 diabetics enrolled at non-elevated LDL-C rather than a hyperlipidemia cohort.
ledger.integrity_note: No retraction or expression of concern found.

ledger.citation: Karlson 2015 (VOYAGER), European Journal of Preventive Cardiology
ledger.finding: VOYAGER pooled RCT analysis quantified dose-dependent atorvastatin LDL-C lowering (e.g. atorvastatin ~15 mg is equipotent to the ~39% LDL-C reduction of rosuvastatin 5 mg; higher atorvastatin doses give larger reductions), confirming dose-dependent LDL-C lowering.
ledger.integrity_note: No retraction or expression of concern found.

claim: Icosapent ethyl (EPA) reduces cardiovascular events in high-risk statin-treated patients with hypertriglyceridemia

ledger.citation: Bhatt DL, et al. Cardiovascular Risk Reduction with Icosapent Ethyl for Hypertriglyceridemia (REDUCE-IT). N Engl J Med. 2019;380(1):11-22.
ledger.finding: In statin-treated patients with elevated triglycerides (135-499 mg/dL) and high CV risk (established CVD or diabetes + risk factors), 4 g/day icosapent ethyl (purified EPA) lowered the primary composite of CV death/MI/stroke/coronary revascularization/unstable angina vs placebo (17.2% vs 22.0%; HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.68-0.83; P<0.001); key secondary composite HR 0.74 (0.65-0.83); CV death also reduced (4.3% vs 5.2%; HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.66-0.98). Median follow-up 4.9 y. POSITIVE. Note: mineral-oil placebo and high-risk/hypertriglyceridemic population limit generalizability to general adults. NCT01492361.
ledger.integrity_note: Amarin-funded pivotal RCT (NEJMoa1812792); mineral-oil placebo controversy noted in later literature but trial itself is peer-reviewed NEJM, no retraction/misconduct. VERIFIED: PMID, n, HR, CIs, NCT all match PubMed record (published online Nov 2018; print 2019;380(1):11-22).

ledger.citation: Nicholls SJ, et al. Effect of High-Dose Omega-3 Fatty Acids vs Corn Oil on Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (STRENGTH). JAMA. 2020;324(22):2268-2280.
ledger.finding: In statin-treated high-CV-risk patients with hypertriglyceridemia and low HDL-C, 4 g/day omega-3 carboxylic acid (EPA+DHA) vs corn oil showed NO difference in the primary MACE composite (12.0% vs 12.2%; HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.90-1.09; P=0.84); trial halted early for futility per prespecified interim. NULL. NCT02104817.
ledger.integrity_note: AstraZeneca-funded (JAMA 2020.22258, PMC7667577); peer-reviewed, prematurely stopped for futility; no integrity concerns. VERIFIED: PMID, n=13078, HR 0.99 (0.90-1.09), P=0.84, corn-oil comparator, NCT all match PubMed.

ledger.citation: Manson JE, et al. Marine n-3 Fatty Acids and Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer (VITAL). N Engl J Med. 2019;380(1):23-32.
ledger.finding: Primary-prevention trial in general US adults (men >=50, women >=55) at usual risk; 1 g/day marine n-3 vs placebo showed NO reduction in major CV events (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.80-1.06; P=0.24) over median 5.3 y. Secondary total-MI signal (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.59-0.90) but null primary. NULL. Best population match to 'general adults'. NCT01169259.
ledger.integrity_note: NIH-funded (NEJMoa1811403, PMC6392053); peer-reviewed NEJM; no integrity concerns. VERIFIED: PMID, n=25871, HR 0.92 (0.80-1.06), P=0.24, median 5.3 y, total-MI HR 0.72, NCT all match PubMed.

ledger.citation: ASCEND Study Collaborative Group (Bowman L, et al.). Effects of n-3 Fatty Acid Supplements in Diabetes Mellitus. N Engl J Med. 2018;379(16):1540-1550.
ledger.finding: In patients with diabetes and no baseline atherosclerotic CVD, 1 g/day n-3 fatty acids vs olive-oil placebo showed NO difference in first serious vascular event (8.9% vs 9.2%; rate ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.87-1.08; P=0.55) over mean 7.4 y. NULL. Diabetic (not general-adult) population. NCT00135226.
ledger.integrity_note: British Heart Foundation-funded (NEJMoa1804989); peer-reviewed NEJM; no integrity concerns. VERIFIED: PMID, n=15480, RR 0.97 (0.87-1.08), P=0.55, mean 7.4 y, olive-oil placebo, NCT00135226 (also ISRCTN60635500) all match PubMed.

ledger.citation: Hu Y, Hu FB, Manson JE. Marine Omega-3 Supplementation and Cardiovascular Disease: An Updated Meta-Analysis of 13 Randomized Controlled Trials Involving 127477 Participants. J Am Heart Assoc. 2019;8(19):e013543.
ledger.finding: Pooled 13 RCTs (127,477 participants; mean treatment 5.0 y). Excluding REDUCE-IT, marine omega-3 was associated with significant reductions in MI (RR 0.92, 0.86-0.99), CHD death (RR 0.92, 0.86-0.98), total CHD (RR 0.95, 0.91-0.99), CVD death (RR 0.93, 0.88-0.99), and total CVD (RR 0.97, 0.94-0.99); associations strengthened with REDUCE-IT included but introduced statistically significant heterogeneity. Linear dose-response for total CVD/major vascular events. Weakly POSITIVE overall; heterogeneity underscores the contested picture.
ledger.integrity_note: NIH-funded (JAHA.119.013543, PMC6806028); peer-reviewed JAHA systematic review/meta-analysis; explicitly flags REDUCE-IT-driven heterogeneity; no integrity concerns. VERIFIED: PMID, n=127477, 13 RCTs, all RRs and CIs match PubMed abstract.

claim: Hydroxychloroquine improves clinical outcomes in COVID-19

gate_trace.detail: excluded 1 study(ies) with documented integrity concerns
trial evidence agrees: no effect (evidence of absence)

ledger.finding: Gautret et al. open-label non-randomized single-arm study (20 treated patients analyzed, 6 co-treated with azithromycin; external/refusal controls) reporting faster nasopharyngeal viral clearance with HCQ +/- azithromycin. This was the flawed early positive signal that drove the HCQ hypothesis; it measured viral load, not clinical outcomes, and was not a controlled outcomes trial. Subject to an ISAC/Elsevier statement / Expression of Concern (April 2020) over inclusion criteria, patient triage and methodology, and fully RETRACTED (retraction notice published in print Jan 2025, IJAA 65(1):107416; online 2024). Design normalized to 'prospective cohort' (single-arm treated + non-randomized comparators, prospective daily viral-load follow-up) — it is NOT a case report.
ledger.integrity_note: Retracted. Retraction notice: 'Retraction notice to Hydroxychloroquine and azithromycin as a treatment of COVID-19...' PMID:39730229, DOI:10.1016/j.ijantimicag.2024.107416 (IJAA 2025;65(1):107416). Retraction cited ethical concerns and methodological flaws: 6 treated patients (incl. 1 death, 3 ICU transfers) dropped from analysis, inconsistent PCR positivity cutoffs between arms, and selective outcome reporting (day-6 vs planned day-7/day-14). Preceded by ISAC Board statement (3 Apr 2020) that the article 'does not meet the Society's expected standard.'

ledger.finding: RECOVERY trial (Horby et al., N Engl J Med; NCT04381936; DOI:10.1056/NEJMoa2022926). Large open-label platform RCT in hospitalized COVID-19: 1561 HCQ vs 3155 usual care. 28-day mortality 27.0% HCQ vs 25.0% usual care (rate ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.97-1.23); HCQ patients less likely to be discharged alive by 28 days (RR 0.90, 0.83-0.98) and, if not ventilated at baseline, higher frequency of invasive ventilation or death. No clinical benefit, trend to harm. Arm closed for lack of efficacy at interim analysis.
ledger.integrity_note: Verified against PubMed abstract; NCT04381936 confirmed as RECOVERY (Univ. of Oxford). DOI:10.1056/NEJMoa2022926.

ledger.finding: WHO SOLIDARITY interim results (Pan et al., N Engl J Med; NCT04315948; DOI:10.1056/NEJMoa2023184). Multinational open-label RCT: death in 104/947 HCQ vs 84/906 control (rate ratio 1.19, 95% CI 0.89-1.59). HCQ had little or no effect on in-hospital mortality, initiation of ventilation, or duration of hospitalization. Null for benefit.
ledger.integrity_note: Verified against PubMed abstract (HCQ arm 104/947 vs 84/906, RR 1.19). NCT04315948 is the ClinicalTrials.gov ID cited by the SOLIDARITY paper (shared registration with DisCoVeRy). DOI:10.1056/NEJMoa2023184.

ledger.finding: ORCHID trial (Self et al., JAMA; NCT04332991; DOI:10.1001/jama.2020.22240). Blinded, placebo-controlled RCT in hospitalized adults (479 randomized; 242 HCQ / 237 placebo), stopped for futility. No difference in COVID Outcomes Scale at day 14 (adjusted OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.73-1.42) and no difference in 28-day mortality (10.4% HCQ vs 10.6% placebo). Null.
ledger.integrity_note: Verified against PubMed abstract; NCT04332991 confirmed as ORCHID (blinded placebo-controlled). DOI:10.1001/jama.2020.22240. n reported as 242 HCQ (479 total randomized).

ledger.finding: CORRECTED CITATION. Axfors et al. international collaborative meta-analysis of RCTs (Nature Communications; DOI:10.1038/s41467-021-22446-z). Pooled all-cause mortality across 26 HCQ RCTs (10,012 patients; dominated by RECOVERY + SOLIDARITY): OR 1.11 (95% CI 1.02-1.20; I2=0%). HCQ associated with increased mortality and no clinical benefit; chloroquine (4 trials, 307 patients) OR 1.77 (0.15-21.13), no benefit.
ledger.integrity_note: CORRECTION: original bundle cited PMID:34800996 / DOI:10.1186/s12879-021-06829-7, which is a DIFFERENT paper (convalescent-plasma meta-analysis, BMC Infect Dis) that does NOT support the finding text. Correct Axfors HCQ meta-analysis is PMID:33859192, Nat Commun 2021;12(1):2349, DOI:10.1038/s41467-021-22446-z. Also corrected: n_int 5480->10012 and '28 HCQ RCTs'->'26 HCQ RCTs' per the verified abstract. (An author correction to this paper exists at PMID:33990619, DOI:10.1038/s41467-021-23559-1 — the primary article remains valid, not retracted.)

claim: Hydroxyethyl starch (HES) is a safe and effective fluid for volume resuscitation in critically ill adults

gate_trace.detail: excluded 1 study(ies) with documented integrity concerns
trial evidence agrees: no effect (evidence of absence)

ledger.citation: Boldt J, et al. Cardiopulmonary bypass priming using a high dose of a balanced hydroxyethyl starch versus an albumin-based priming strategy. Anesth Analg. 2009;109(6):1752-62. RETRACTED. DOI 10.1213/ANE.0b013e3181b5a24b
ledger.finding: Joachim Boldt RCT: 6% HES 130/0.42 vs albumin priming for cardiopulmonary bypass in 50 CABG patients; falsely reported HES REDUCED inflammation (IL-6/IL-10), endothelial damage (ICAM-1), renal tubular injury (a-GST, NGAL) and better preserved coagulation/platelet function - i.e. made HES look protective and safe. FABRICATED: retracted by Anesthesia & Analgesia (Dec 2010, PMID:21106980); the 2014 editor's note (PMID:25329035) names this exact paper and states the Klinikum Ludwigshafen investigation 'determined that the study was fabricated' (no IRB approval, no informed consent, missing/fabricated data). Cardiac-surgery CPB-priming population, not general critically-ill ICU resuscitation.
ledger.integrity_note: RETRACTED / FABRICATED. PubMed article-type flag: 'Retracted Publication'. Retraction notice: Shafer SL. Notice of retraction. Anesth Analg. 2010;111(6):1567 (PMID:21106980, DOI 10.1213/ANE.0b013e3182040b99). Reaffirmed by editor's note PMID:25329035 (2014) which names this HES-vs-albumin CPB-priming paper and states the Klinikum Ludwigshafen investigation found it fabricated. Part of the ~88/89-article joint retraction (18 editors-in-chief, 2011); Boldt is anesthesiology's retraction record-holder (>180 papers). His fabricated trials systematically made HES appear safe/effective; excluding them flips the honest verdict to harm (Not Supported).

ledger.citation: Brunkhorst FM, et al. Intensive insulin therapy and pentastarch resuscitation in severe sepsis. N Engl J Med. 2008;358(2):125-39. NCT00135473. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa070716
ledger.finding: VISEP trial. In 537 evaluable patients with severe sepsis, 10% pentastarch (HES 200/0.5) vs modified Ringer's lactate. HES caused higher rates of acute renal failure and renal-replacement therapy, with toxicity increasing with cumulative dose; trial stopped early for safety. Authors: 'As used in this study, HES was harmful, and its toxicity increased with accumulating doses.' (NCT00135473)

ledger.citation: Perner A, et al. Hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.42 versus Ringer's acetate in severe sepsis. N Engl J Med. 2012;367(2):124-34. NCT00962156. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1204242
ledger.finding: 6S trial. 804 patients with severe sepsis randomized to 6% HES 130/0.42 (Tetraspan) vs Ringer's acetate. At 90 days, death 51% (HES) vs 43% (Ringer's), relative risk 1.17 (95% CI 1.01-1.36, P=0.03); more renal-replacement therapy (22% vs 16%, RR 1.35, 95% CI 1.01-1.80, P=0.04) and a trend to more severe bleeding (10% vs 6%). HES increased death and RRT.

ledger.citation: Myburgh JA, et al. Hydroxyethyl starch or saline for fluid resuscitation in intensive care (CHEST). N Engl J Med. 2012;367(20):1901-11. NCT00935168. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1209759
ledger.finding: CHEST trial. 7000 ICU patients randomized to 6% HES 130/0.4 (Voluven) vs 0.9% saline. No mortality benefit (90-day death 18.0% vs 17.0%, RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.96-1.18, NS) but MORE renal-replacement therapy (7.0% vs 5.8%, RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.00-1.45, P=0.04) and significantly more adverse events (5.3% vs 2.8%, P<0.001). HES gave no benefit and more renal harm in general critically ill adults.

ledger.citation: Haase N, Perner A, et al. Hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.38-0.45 versus crystalloid or albumin in patients with sepsis: systematic review with meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis. BMJ. 2013;346:f839. DOI 10.1136/bmj.f839
ledger.finding: Systematic review + meta-analysis + trial sequential analysis of 9 RCTs (3456 sepsis patients) of HES 130/0.38-0.45 vs crystalloid or albumin. HES increased renal-replacement therapy (RR 1.36, 1.08-1.72), red-cell transfusion (RR 1.29, 1.13-1.48) and serious adverse events (RR 1.30, 1.02-1.67); in low-risk-of-bias trials the relative risk of death was 1.11 (1.00-1.23). Authors: 'unlikely that HES 130/0.38-0.45 provides overall clinical benefit for patients with sepsis.' Clean, post-Boldt evidence synthesis.

ledger.citation: Serpa Neto A, et al. Fluid resuscitation with hydroxyethyl starches in patients with sepsis is associated with an increased incidence of acute kidney injury and use of renal replacement therapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Crit Care. 2013;29(1):185.e1-7. DOI 10.1016/j.jcrc.2013.09.031
ledger.finding: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 trials (4624 septic patients), HES vs crystalloid. HES increased acute kidney injury (RR 1.24, 1.13-1.36), need for renal-replacement therapy (RR 1.36, 1.17-1.57), red-cell transfusion (RR 1.14, 1.01-1.93) and 90-day mortality (RR 1.14, 1.04-1.26). Authors favor crystalloids over HES for sepsis resuscitation.

claim: Metformin reduces cancer incidence in adults without diabetes

gate_trace.detail: trial evidence agrees: no effect (evidence of absence)

ledger.finding: In the Diabetes Prevention Program RCT of adults at high diabetes risk (non-diabetic, impaired glucose tolerance at randomization), metformin 850 mg BID did not reduce total cancer incidence vs placebo over a median 21 years (546 first cancers; HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.73-1.10).
ledger.integrity_note: No retraction or expression of concern (verified). Trial = NCT00004992 (DPP/DPPOS), enrollment 3,234, confirmed on ClinicalTrials.gov. Only bundle row with a true non-diabetic population and RCT-tier design — load-bearing for the verdict.

ledger.finding: Collaborative meta-analysis of randomized trials found no reduction in cancer with metformin (summary RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.82-1.26), directly refuting the ~one-third reduction seen in observational studies.
ledger.integrity_note: No retraction/EoC (verified). Trials mostly enrolled diabetic patients, so population match to non-diabetic adults is only partial — honestly flagged false.

ledger.finding: Emulating a target trial removed the apparent protective signal: primary 6-year cancer risk difference (metformin vs no metformin, in individuals WITH diabetes) was ~0 (ITT -0.2%, 95% CI -1.6% to 1.3%); a secondary emulation regardless of diabetes status was also near-zero, whereas naive observational methods appeared strongly protective.
ledger.integrity_note: No retraction/EoC (verified). CORRECTED population_match true->false: the headline emulation is restricted to individuals with diabetes; only a secondary analysis is diabetes-agnostic. Explicitly shows the observational protective signal is an analytic artifact.

ledger.finding: Meta-analysis of 6 RCTs found no significant association between metformin and skin cancer (melanoma OR 0.82, 0.27-2.43; total skin cancer OR 0.71, 0.42-1.20); parallel cohort meta-analysis also null.
ledger.integrity_note: No retraction/EoC (verified). Diabetes/prediabetes populations; site-specific (skin), so population_match false.

ledger.finding: The naive observational signal: pooled all-cancer incidence RR 0.67 (95% CI 0.53-0.85) favoring metformin, but derived mainly from cohort/case-control studies in diabetic patients; authors themselves flag need for RCTs.
ledger.integrity_note: No retraction/EoC (verified). Represents the confounded observational signal later refuted by RCTs/TTE; diabetic population only, so population_match false. Normalized to 'systematic review' (pools observational data, not RCTs).

ledger.finding: Observational meta-analysis reporting reduced pancreatic cancer risk with metformin (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.46-0.86) in type 2 diabetes — a site-specific instance of the same confounded observational signal, from cohort/case-control data only.
ledger.integrity_note: No retraction/EoC (verified). Purely observational; diabetic population; susceptible to time-related/immortal-time bias. Normalized to 'systematic review' (pools observational data, not RCTs).
